Content: Database servers (Finance-DB, Customer-DB). Criticality: CRITICAL. Allowed Ports: 443, 22, 3306/5432 only. Behavior: No outbound internet access, encrypted internal communication only.
Web servers (Web-Frontend, API-Gateway). Criticality: HIGH. Allowed Ports: 80, 443, 22. Behavior: High inbound traffic, limited outbound to internal services only.
Mail servers (SMTP-Server, Exchange). Criticality: HIGH. Allowed Ports: 25, 465, 587, 993, 995. Behavior: Email traffic patterns, expected large volumes during business hours.
Domain controllers (DC1, DC2). Criticality: CRITICAL. Allowed Ports: 53, 88, 135, 139, 389, 445, 464, 636. Behavior: Authentication traffic, no direct internet access.
Employee workstations. Criticality: MEDIUM. Behavior: Standard web browsing, email, file access during business hours.
Guest WiFi network (192.168.100.x). Criticality: LOW. Behavior: High traffic volume expected, limited internal access.
IoT devices (Cameras, Sensors). Criticality: LOW. Behavior: Minimal bandwidth, specific communication patterns to central management.
Network infrastructure (Routers, Switches). Criticality: HIGH. Behavior: Management traffic only, SNMP monitoring.

DNS-based attacks via UDP with interrupted connections. Indicators: Small payloads ~114 bytes, very high rates >200K.
Exploitation attempts via unknown protocols (3pc, a/n, aes-sp3-d). Indicators: 2 packets, 200 bytes, interrupted connections.
Sequential port scanning across ranges 7000-9000. Indicator of C2 communication initiation or reconnaissance.

High-volume SMTP traffic with unusual packet ratios. Indicators: >100 source packets, >30 dest packets, >100KB data.
SSL/TLS connections with abnormal duration and data volumes. Indicators: >50 packets each direction, >13 second duration.
OSPF protocol abuse for malicious communication. Indicators: 44+ packets, >8KB data, interrupted or request states.
SCTP protocol exploitation with large data transfers. Indicators: >35 packets, >35KB source bytes, live connections.
Backdoor communication patterns using various protocols with specific byte signatures and timing.
Reconnaissance activity including port scanning, network enumeration, and service discovery attempts.
DoS attack patterns with high packet rates, connection flooding, or resource exhaustion attempts.
Worm propagation signatures with self-replicating network behavior and lateral movement indicators.
Fuzzer activity with malformed packets, unusual protocol usage, or testing patterns.
Shellcode injection attempts with executable payloads and memory manipulation indicators.
Failed login attempts <5 on LOW criticality assets are classified as BENIGN.
Failed login attempts >5 on any asset are classified as SUSPICIOUS.
ANY unexpected outbound connections from CRITICAL assets are ZERO-DAY candidates until proven otherwise.
Data transfers >1GB from database servers to external IPs are ZERO-DAY candidates.
Communications on non-standard ports from CRITICAL/HIGH assets require SUSPICIOUS classification.
Known attack signature matches should be classified as SUSPICIOUS and verified through CorrectiveRAG.
Encrypted traffic on unusual ports (not 443, 993, 995) from internal assets is SUSPICIOUS.
Multiple protocol violations from same source IP within 1 hour indicate SUSPICIOUS activity.
Traffic patterns deviating >3 standard deviations from normal baselines are ZERO-DAY candidates.
Cross-network communications violating network segmentation policies are ZERO-DAY candidates.
Privilege escalation attempts or admin account abuse are always SUSPICIOUS minimum.
Lateral movement patterns across multiple assets indicate ZERO-DAY or advanced persistent threat.
TCP normal behavior: 1-5 packets per direction, <1KB typical payload, connection durations <10 seconds for most services.
UDP normal behavior: 1-2 packets, <500 bytes payload, rates <1000 for most services except streaming.
HTTP normal: 23 source packets, 83 destination packets, 3-104KB data exchange, <2 second duration.
SMTP normal: Variable packet count, up to 132KB source data, <3 second duration for message transfer.
SSH normal: Low packet count, minimal data for administration, authentication bursts followed by idle.
DNS normal: 2 packets typical query/response, 57-114 bytes payload, sub-second response times.
FTP normal: Control channel <1KB, data channel variable based on file size, separate connections.
SSL normal: Handshake 10-20 packets, then variable data based on application, encrypt overhead 5-15%.
DHCP normal: 4 packet DISCOVER/OFFER/REQUEST/ACK sequence, 200-300 byte payloads.
ARP normal: Broadcast requests, unicast responses, 42-60 byte frames, periodic refresh.
Port knocking sequences (7000, 8000, 9000) indicate C2 channel establishment attempts.
Data exfiltration via DNS tunneling shows high query volumes with encoded payloads.
Lateral movement using WMI, PSExec, or SMB with admin credentials from compromised workstations.
Cryptocurrency mining malware shows sustained high CPU usage and pool communication patterns.
Ransomware behavior includes file encryption activity, network share scanning, and ransom note deployment.
APT indicators include long-term persistence, scheduled task creation, and periodic data staging.
Web shell deployment through vulnerable applications with subsequent command execution attempts.
SQL injection attempts via web applications with database error responses or timing delays.
Buffer overflow exploits targeting specific services with crafted payloads and ROP chains.
Zero-day exploits show novel attack vectors without known signatures or CVE references.
Insider threats exhibit abnormal data access patterns, privilege abuse, or policy violations.
Supply chain attacks through compromised software updates or third-party integrations.
BENIGN: Routine business operations, expected user activities, normal system maintenance, approved software installations.
SUSPICIOUS: Known attack patterns, policy violations, unusual but explainable activities, signature matches requiring verification.
ZERO-DAY: Novel attack patterns, behavior contradicting asset profiles, unknown threat vectors, advanced evasion techniques.
ARP baseline: Minimal packets (1-2), 42-60 bytes, local network only, periodic refresh every 4 hours.
OSPF baseline: Routing updates, Hello packets every 10 seconds, LSA flooding during topology changes.
TCP baseline: 3-way handshake, data transfer, 4-way close, connection state tracking, sequence numbers.
UDP baseline: Connectionless, single request/response, DNS queries, SNMP polls, minimal state.
SCTP baseline: Multi-homing support, stream control, heartbeat messages, association management.
HTTP baseline: Request/response pattern, GET/POST methods, headers <2KB, response codes 200-400 range.
SMTP baseline: HELO/EHLO greeting, AUTH if required, MAIL FROM/RCPT TO envelope, DATA message transfer.
SSH baseline: Version negotiation, key exchange, authentication, encrypted channel, keep-alive messages.
SSL/TLS baseline: Handshake negotiation, certificate exchange, cipher selection, encrypted application data.
DNS baseline: Query/response, A/AAAA/CNAME records, recursive/iterative resolution, 512 byte UDP limit.
Web services: HTTP/HTTPS on ports 80/443, expected response times <3 seconds, standard status codes.
Email services: SMTP/IMAP/POP3, authentication required, message size limits, spam filtering.
File services: FTP/SFTP/SMB, authentication required, access controls, transfer logging.
Database services: MySQL/PostgreSQL/MSSQL, encrypted connections preferred, query logging enabled.
Directory services: LDAP/AD, authentication traffic, policy distribution, replication between DCs.
Remote access: RDP/VNC/SSH, strong authentication required, session logging, time limits.
Network services: DHCP/DNS/NTP, infrastructure support, monitoring required, redundancy configured.
Backup services: Scheduled operations, encrypted transfers, integrity verification, retention policies.
Unusual data volumes: >10x normal baseline for service indicates potential data exfiltration or DDoS.
Abnormal connection patterns: Persistent connections where short-lived expected, or vice versa.
Geographic anomalies: Connections from unexpected countries or impossible travel times between logins.
Time-based anomalies: Activity during off-hours without authorization or scheduled maintenance.
Protocol anomalies: Mismatched protocol usage, tunneling detection, or covert channels.
Behavioral anomalies: User actions inconsistent with role, access patterns, or historical behavior.
Performance anomalies: Response times, throughput, or resource usage outside normal parameters.
Frequency anomalies: Event counts, rates, or intervals significantly different from baseline.
Source IP analysis: Same source IP with >50 different destination IPs in 5 minutes indicates scanning behavior.
Port analysis: Source ports <1024 from non-privileged hosts indicate potential privilege escalation or spoofing.
Destination port analysis: Connections to ports >50000 or non-standard service ports require investigation.
Protocol analysis: Non-TCP/UDP protocols (OSPF, SCTP, ARP) from end-user hosts are suspicious.
Connection state analysis: High ratio of INT (interrupted) states indicates failed connection attempts or scanning.
Duration analysis: Connections <0.001 seconds or >3600 seconds deviate from normal application behavior.
Byte transfer analysis: Source bytes >1MB with destination bytes <1KB indicates potential data exfiltration.
TTL analysis: TTL values <30 or >128 may indicate packet crafting or routing anomalies.
Packet loss analysis: >10% packet loss (sloss/dloss) in internal networks indicates network issues or attacks.
Load analysis: Source load >10Mbps from single host indicates potential DDoS participation or compromise.
Packet count analysis: >1000 packets in single flow indicates bulk transfer or potential attack traffic.
Window size analysis: TCP window sizes <1024 or >65535 may indicate stack fingerprinting or evasion.
Sequence number analysis: TCP sequence number patterns can reveal OS fingerprinting attempts.
Packet size analysis: Mean packet sizes <64 or >1500 bytes indicate potential protocol abuse or tunneling.
HTTP transaction depth >10 indicates potential HTTP pipelining abuse or application layer attacks.
HTTP response body >10MB without corresponding application need indicates potential data exfiltration.
Jitter analysis: Network jitter >100ms indicates potential congestion, routing issues, or quality degradation.
Inter-packet timing: Consistent timing patterns may indicate automated tools or bot behavior.
TCP RTT analysis: Round-trip times >500ms for local networks indicate potential network issues or man-in-middle.
SYN-ACK timing: >100ms between SYN and SYN-ACK indicates potential SYN flood or network congestion.
ACK-DATA timing: >50ms between ACK and DATA indicates application delays or processing issues.
Same IP/Port analysis: Source and destination IP/ports being identical indicates potential loopback or reflection attacks.
State-TTL correlation: Abnormal TTL values for specific connection states indicate potential evasion techniques.
HTTP method analysis: Unusual HTTP methods or >100 flows with same method indicate potential web attacks.
FTP login analysis: Multiple failed FTP login attempts indicate brute force or credential stuffing attacks.
FTP command analysis: >50 FTP commands in single session indicate potential automated exploitation or data theft.
Service connection analysis: >20 connections to same service from single source indicate potential service abuse.
Destination connection analysis: >100 connections to single destination indicate potential DDoS or focused attack.
Source connection analysis: >100 connections from single source indicate potential infected host or attack tool.
Port destination analysis: >50 connections to same destination port indicate potential service-specific attacks.
Address pair analysis: >10 connections between same source-destination pair indicate potential persistent compromise.
ACC (Accepted): Normal for established connections, abnormal if >1000 concurrent for single source.
CLO (Closed): Normal connection termination, suspicious if immediate after establishment without data transfer.
CON (Connected): Active data transfer state, monitor for duration and data volume anomalies.
ECO (Echo): ICMP echo state, suspicious if high volume or from internal hosts to external networks.
ECR (Echo Reply): ICMP echo reply, monitor for timing patterns indicating reconnaissance.
FIN (Finished): Normal TCP termination, suspicious if immediate or without proper handshake sequence.
INT (Interrupted): Connection interrupted, high rates indicate scanning, failed exploits, or network issues.
MAS (Masquerading): Indicates potential IP spoofing or masquerading behavior, always suspicious.
PAR (Partial): Incomplete connection establishment, high rates indicate SYN flood or scanning.
REQ (Request): Connection request state, monitor for request/response ratios and timing.
RST (Reset): Connection reset, high rates indicate port scanning or service disruption attempts.
TST (Test): Test connections, should be minimal in production networks, investigate all occurrences.
TXD (Transaction Done): Transaction completed, monitor for timing and data volume consistency.
URH (Urgent): Urgent data flag set, rare in normal traffic, investigate for potential evasion techniques.
URN (Urgent No): Urgent flag cleared, monitor in context of URH states for protocol manipulation.
HTTP service: Normal GET/POST ratio 3:1, >10:1 indicates potential web scraping or reconnaissance.
FTP service: Normal login followed by data transfer, multiple logins without transfer indicate brute force.
SMTP service: Normal message size 1-10MB, >50MB indicates potential data exfiltration via email.
SSH service: Normal session 5-60 minutes, >4 hours indicates potential persistent access or tunneling.
DNS service: Normal query/response 1:1 ratio, >5:1 indicates potential DNS tunneling or amplification.
FTP-DATA service: Should correlate with FTP control channel, standalone data connections are suspicious.
IRC service: Rare in corporate networks, any IRC traffic should be investigated for C2 communication.
Unknown services (-): High volume of unknown service traffic indicates potential covert channels.
Fuzzers: Characterized by malformed packets, unusual protocol usage, rapid connection attempts to test vulnerabilities.
Analysis: Network reconnaissance including port scanning, service enumeration, OS fingerprinting, and vulnerability scanning.
Backdoors: Persistent access mechanisms with periodic beaconing, often using encrypted or obfuscated communication.
DoS: High packet rates, connection flooding, resource exhaustion targeting availability of services or network.
Exploits: Targeted attacks against specific vulnerabilities, often with unusual packet patterns or payload signatures.
Generic: Basic malicious activity not fitting other categories, often automated or scripted attacks.
Reconnaissance: Information gathering activities including network mapping, service discovery, and target profiling.
Shellcode: Code injection attempts with executable payloads designed to gain control of target systems.
Worms: Self-propagating malware with network scanning and automated exploitation of discovered vulnerabilities.
Normal inter-packet arrival: 1-100ms for interactive applications, 0.1-1ms for bulk transfers.
Abnormal jitter patterns: >50ms variation indicates network congestion or potential quality of service attacks.
Suspicious timing regularity: Exactly timed intervals indicate automated tools or bot behavior.
Connection timing: <1ms establishment indicates local connections, >1000ms indicates distant or slow connections.
Data transfer timing: Consistent with connection bandwidth and latency, deviations indicate potential issues.
Normal packet ratios: Bidirectional flows should have response packets, unidirectional may indicate scanning.
Abnormal byte ratios: >100:1 source to destination ratio indicates potential command injection or data exfiltration.
Connection persistence: Long-duration connections normal for some applications, monitor for data volume consistency.
Flow termination patterns: Normal applications close connections cleanly, abnormal termination indicates potential attacks.
TCP flow characteristics: Three-way handshake, data transfer, four-way close. Deviations indicate evasion or attacks.
UDP flow characteristics: Stateless request/response. Persistent UDP flows may indicate tunneling or abuse.
ICMP flow characteristics: Echo request/reply, error messages. High volumes indicate reconnaissance or attacks.
Internal network baselines: Establish normal communication patterns between network segments and critical assets.
External network baselines: Monitor outbound connections for data volume, timing, and destination patterns.
Cross-network communication: Inter-VLAN traffic should match business requirements and security policies.
Bandwidth utilization: Establish per-host and per-service baselines for normal bandwidth consumption patterns.
User activity patterns: Establish normal working hours, application usage, and data access patterns per user role.
Host activity patterns: Normal process communications, service startups, and resource utilization per host type.
Application behavioral baselines: Normal transaction volumes, response times, and error rates per application.
Seasonal and temporal patterns: Account for business cycles, maintenance windows, and scheduled activities.
